t: ‘Worse than anyone feared’: how Victorian Labor unravelled after 12 years in government
lede: Halfway through the election campaign, the recriminations had already begun, with accusations that Ben Carroll made fatal mistakes that cost the party the election

img.cap: ‘There didn’t seem to be a strategy behind anything,’ says one MP of Ben Carroll’s election campaign. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP

p: It was the moment that, in hindsight, many within Labor believe Ben Carroll lost the Victorian election.
At his first press conference as premier in late July, Carroll told reporters: “I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan.”

Long known to dislike Andrews, and desperate to leave behind the corruption allegations that had dogged Allan for two years and contributed to a crash in the party’s primary vote, Carroll sought to distance himself as much as possible from the previous 12 years of Labor rule.
But for one party insider, whose campaign experience stretches back to the election of John Cain in 1982, it was a “fatal flaw”.

“From day one, he boxed himself in. He said some things that completely constrained what he could do from there on in,” they said. “And then, once trouble starts, it has a habit of escalating and feeding on itself endlessly. It’s a tragedy, really.”
Midway through the campaign, the recriminations began.
“This is the worst campaign I’ve ever seen,” one minister said, just two weeks into the campaign.
By the final week, most MPs were despondent.
“Anyone wanting to know how to run a successful political campaign and messaging should just look at Victorian Labor and our leadership over the past 100 days and do exactly the opposite,” one said.
On Saturday night, the mood had become catatonic: “This is worse than anyone feared.”
Guardian Australia has spoken to more than a dozen Labor figures who acknowledge that winning an unprecedented fourth consecutive term was always going to be an extraordinary challenge.

But few anticipated the scale of the defeat – or the speed with which the party’s fortunes would unravel. At the 2022 election, Labor won 56 seats. By late Saturday night, Guardian Australia had called just six for the party. Many party figures said Carroll should carry much of the blame for the wipeout.
“From that very first press conference, the new leadership made people feel we should be ashamed of our government and all we had achieved,” a former minister said.
“For the first time in my life I took my Labor T-shirt off when I went to have lunch during prepoll. I just didn’t want to draw attention to myself. It feels like a tarnished brand.”
Those close to Carroll, though, believe he will ultimately be remembered as the Labor leader who started the hard work of cleaning up the party and restoring its credibility.

“If he did nothing else but put a little bit of integrity and trust back into elected officials, then to me, that is a win, irrespective of the result,” Philip Dalidakis, Carroll’s close friend and former cabinet colleague, said.
Asked where Carroll went wrong, most MPs begin with his first few weeks as premier.
Determined to “reset” the relationship with the business community, Carroll in August paused debate on legislation to enshrine the right to work from home, just as the bill was

The olive branch was unreciprocated – business lobby groups weren’t willing to consult on the bill and wanted it gone. Amendments were made and it was brought back to the upper house, where the Coalition and crossbench teamed up to refer it to an inquiry,

p.t: stalling the laws before the election

p: . A Coalition government won’t seek to revive them.

Even Labor MPs who questioned the need for the laws were demoralised by the outcome. They said it was particularly popular with women – a demographic that had flocked to the party under Andrews but began to walk away under Allan.
Then there was Carroll’s focus on crime. In September, he
, giving police and protective services powers to stop and scan people using handheld metal detectors, reversing the government’s previous rejected of a similar Coalition proposal.
The left caucus met after the announcement and several MPs unloaded, according to multiple sources present.
One MP said: “There didn’t appear to be a strategy behind it. This was before we realised there didn’t seem to be a strategy behind anything.”

p: The focus on crime continued throughout the election campaign, with a week spent announcing commitments such as

p.t: a $204m “tough love”plan for low-level youth offenders

p: and the reopening of police stations that had closed under Labor’s watch.

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist turned pollster with Redbridge, said the strategy was a “disaster” on two grounds. It highlighted the party’s failure over two years to tackle the rising crime rate and, even more significantly, it alienated inner-city voters.

Samaras said, according to his polling, Labor went into the campaign on a 25% primary vote, having already lost about half a million voters to either the Coalition or One Nation. During the campaign, it dropped to 20%. On election night, it was even lower.

“If you look at where that 5% has gone, it’s gone to the Greens, it’s gone to the Socialists and it’s been predominately women who are dismayed by the idea of locking up children for shoplifting,” Samaras said.
Dalidakis disputes the criticism. He said it would have been an “insult to the Victorian public” for Carroll to ignore an issue that voters identified as a top concern.
This was further highlighted by a series of stabbings in the CBD during the campaign.
Some MPs on the right believe the government’s biggest mistake on crime came in 2023, when it
to reduce the number of people who are remanded in custody for low-level offending. It followed a coronial inquest into the

p.t: death in custody of First Nations woman Veronica Nelson

p: after she was arrested for shoplifting.
One MP said the loosening of the laws was followed by an increase in offending,

. “By the time the CFMEU allegations came to light, there was already a public perception already that we were soft on crime,” they said. “The public felt that we were not on their side, we were on the side of the youth offender that was given bail or the bikie on the construction site.”
Midway through the campaign, Carroll returned to more familiar territory for Labor: health. But even on this front MPs were uncomfortable with the strategy.

Labor focused heavily on the idea that a Coalition government would “Americanise healthcare”, with Carroll even handing out mock medical bills claiming giving birth would cost $20,000, an MRI $10,000 and Ventolin $120.
Some MPs were unwilling to repeat the lines.
“It seemed really desperate, which makes no sense to me because we have a really good story to tell in the health space,” one said.

MPs on both the left and right were also perplexed by the relative absence of women’s health from the campaign, despite significant achievements over the term. When the campaign briefly turned to the issue, it was to announce a promise to make abortion care free and warn that reproductive rights could be under threat under a “Liberal-One Nation Coalition”.
The Liberal leader Jess Wilson, quickly matched the commitment and called out Labor for
. Labor MPs privately agreed with her.
“Abortion is not a contested space in Australia,” one said. “How can he [Carroll] say Jess Wilson and the Liberals are Americanising healthcare when he is Americanising the political debate?”

The MP said the move could have contributed to Carroll losing his seat of Niddrie, which is the most Christian electorate in Victoria. Other faith communities, they said, were also upset by the approach.

Others said Carroll made several other “own goals”, including cuts to disability support for public schools on the eve of the campaign and the decision to use a $1.3bn dividend from WorkSafe to prop up the state’s finances. Both drew a chorus of criticism, significantly from unions,

p.t: many of which had already decided to sit out the campaign

p: MPs also point to Carroll’s performance in the only debate of the campaign – where his delivery was wooden and he

p.t: refused to utter Andrews or Allan’s name

p: – after he had pressured Wilson to take part. Morale was so low that several MPs said they couldn’t even watch.
“He’s just a bit odd, a bit awkward – and that’s not to say he’s a bad guy, he’s a thoroughly decent man – but he wasn’t up to the gargantuan task,” one MP said.
A senior campaign source said the election was always going to be challenging, thanks to rising interest rates and inflation and the push against incumbent governments across the globe.
“Not to make excuses, but the Democrats flipped fucking Texas,” they said.
Many in Labor lay the blame at Allan for failing to adequately address corruption on the Big Build, which was first reported in 2024. In July, Allan
the multibillion dollar government infrastructure program but refused to call a royal commission.

p.t: Carroll announced it once he became premier

p: , with hearings airing damaging allegations during the campaign.

Those on Labor’s campaign said the allegations surrounding the state’s major projects tainted them. Carroll didn’t hold a single press conference at Footscray hospital, the Metro Tunnel or the West Gate Tunnel during the campaign.
A senior source said the campaign tested advertising on Labor’s achievements, including the projects and received a poor response.
“People felt gaslit. People said, ‘You can’t paint us a rosy picture. You fucked this state and we have no money,’” they said.
Samaras said the loss was 12 years in the making.
“The broth has been spoilt but there’s been three chefs. They all had a role,” he said. “You don’t get a result like this purely because of the campaign.”
